did_you_know.text: In the opening verse, the LORD describes himself as available and responsive even to those who did not seek him, offering his presence to a nation that is not called by his name.
The LORD describes his patience with the words, “I have spread out my hands all day long,” even as the people continue on a path that is not good and follow their own thoughts.
The people are described as provoking the LORD through worship practices in various places: sacrificing in gardens and burning incense on bricks.

The illustration of the grape cluster and its juice teaches about a faithful remnant: when new wine is found in a cluster, it should not be destroyed. Therefore, the LORD promises not to destroy everything for the sake of his servants.
Sharon and the Valley of Achor, representing regions of the land, are described in the future as places for pasture—Sharon as a fold for flocks and the Valley of Achor as a resting place for cattle.

The prophet contrasts those who forsake the LORD with those who serve him: those who forsake the LORD set a table for Gad and fill cups of mixed wine for Meni, while the LORD’s servants will receive blessing.
Punishment and reward are presented in sharp contrast: the LORD’s servants will eat, drink, and rejoice, while the sinners will hunger, thirst, and be put to shame.
The LORD promises to create “new heavens and a new earth,” so that the former troubles will not be remembered or even come to mind.
The description of the new reality includes exceptionally long lives: a young man is considered to have died at a hundred, while a sinner who reaches a hundred is still regarded as accursed.

The vision of peace also includes the animal world: the wolf and the lamb will graze together, the lion will eat straw, and the serpent will cause no harm; no one will hurt or destroy anywhere on the LORD’s holy mountain.
